title: Finding the Duplicate in an Array of N Plus One Integers

phrases.explanation: To step through a specific test case to demonstrate how the algorithm works
A constraint meaning you cannot sort or change elements in place

phrases.phrase: trade off between time and space
phrases.explanation: Choosing to use more memory to gain speed, or vice versa
To find a loop in a sequence where values eventually repeat
To reduce the range of possible answers with each step

technical_terms.definition: An algorithm technique to find loops in a linked structure, often using two pointers moving at different speeds
A two-pointer cycle detection algorithm where one pointer moves one step and the other moves two steps at a time
A data structure that stores unique elements and supports constant time lookup and insertion
If n plus one items are placed into n containers, at least one container must hold more than one item
A linked list formed by treating array values as pointers to the next index

concept: Given an array of n plus one integers where each integer is between 1 and n inclusive, find the single duplicate number. The array must not be modified and only constant extra space should be used for the optimal solution.

solutions.label: HashSet Lookup
solutions.summary: Iterate through the array, adding each number to a HashSet. If a number is already in the set, it is the duplicate.

solutions.label: Binary Search on Value Range
solutions.summary: Binary search on the value range one to n. For each midpoint, count how many numbers are at or below it. If the count exceeds the midpoint, the duplicate is in the lower half.

solutions.label: Floyd's Cycle Detection
solutions.summary: Treat the array as an implicit linked list where each value points to the next index. Use slow and fast pointers to detect and locate the cycle entry point, which is the duplicate.

sections.title: Understanding the Problem
sections.diagram:
graph TD
    subgraph Input["Array of 5 elements (n=4)"]
        A["Index 0: 1"] --> B["Index 1: 3"]
        B --> C["Index 2: 4"]
        C --> D["Index 3: 2"]
        D --> E["Index 4: 3"]
    end
    E -->|"Duplicate found"| F["Answer: 3"]
    style F fill:#f87171,color:#fff
    style E fill:#f87171,color:#fff

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Here's the problem. You're given an array containing n plus one integers, and every integer is in the range from one to n. By the pigeonhole principle, there must be at least one duplicate. Your task is to find that duplicate number.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Understood. So if the array has five elements, each value is between one and four, and exactly one value appears more than once. Can I ask a few clarifying questions? Is there always exactly one duplicate, or could there be multiple?

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: There is guaranteed to be exactly one duplicate number, but it could appear more than twice. The array will always have at least two elements. Also, you must not modify the original array.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Got it. So for example, given the array one, three, four, two, three, the answer is three. I just return the duplicate value itself. Are there any space constraints?

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Ideally, aim for constant extra space. But let's start with whatever approach comes to mind first and optimize from there.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Alright. Let me summarize: I have an array of n plus one integers, values from one to n, I cannot modify it, and I need to find the one repeated value. Let me start with a straightforward approach.

sections.title: HashSet Lookup
sections.diagram:
graph LR
    subgraph Process["Scan array: [1, 3, 4, 2, 3]"]
        S1["1 → add to set"] --> S2["3 → add to set"]
        S2 --> S3["4 → add to set"]
        S3 --> S4["2 → add to set"]
        S4 --> S5["3 → already in set!"]
    end
    S5 --> R["Return 3"]
    style S5 fill:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style R fill:#60a5fa,color:#fff

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: My first idea is to use a HashSet. I iterate through the array and try to add each number to the set. If the add operation returns false, that number is already in the set, so it's the duplicate.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Walking through our example, one, three, four, two, three. I add one, three, four, two successfully. When I reach three again, it's already in the set, so I return three.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: That works. What's the time and space complexity?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Time is O of n since I scan the array once. Space is also O of n for the HashSet. It's simple and correct, but uses linear extra space. Can I try to do better on space?

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Yes, please try to reduce the space usage.

sections.title: Binary Search on Value Range
sections.diagram:
graph TD
    subgraph BS["Binary search on range 1 to 4"]
        R1["low=1, high=4, mid=2"] --> C1{"Count of values ≤ 2: 2"}
        C1 -->|"2 ≤ 2 → duplicate in upper half"| R2["low=3, high=4, mid=3"]
        R2 --> C2{"Count of values ≤ 3: 4"}
        C2 -->|"4 > 3 → duplicate in lower half"| R3["low=3, high=3"]
    end
    R3 --> RES["Return 3"]
    style R2 fill:#a78bfa,color:#fff
    style RES fill:#a78bfa,color:#fff

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: I can binary search on the value range instead of the array indices. The values go from one to n. I pick a midpoint and count how many array elements are less than or equal to that midpoint. If the count exceeds the midpoint, the duplicate must be in the lower half of the range.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: For our example with values one to four, I set low to one and high to four. Mid is two. I count elements less than or equal to two: that's one and two, so two elements. Two is not greater than two, so the duplicate is in the upper half. I set low to three.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Now low is three, high is four, mid is three. I count elements less than or equal to three: one, three, two, three. That's four elements, which exceeds three. So the duplicate is in the lower half. High becomes three. Low equals high, so I return three.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Good. The time complexity here is O of n log n because you scan the entire array for each binary search step. Space is O of one. Can you achieve O of n time with O of one space?

sections.title: Floyd's Cycle Detection
sections.diagram:
graph LR
    subgraph IL["Implicit linked list from [1,3,4,2,3]"]
        I0["0"] -->|"nums[0]=1"| I1["1"]
        I1 -->|"nums[1]=3"| I3["3"]
        I3 -->|"nums[3]=2"| I2["2"]
        I2 -->|"nums[2]=4"| I4["4"]
        I4 -->|"nums[4]=3"| I3B["3 (cycle!)"]
    end
    I3B --> RES["Cycle entry = 3"]
    style I3B fill:#fb923c,color:#fff
    style RES fill:#fb923c,color:#fff
    style I3 fill:#fb923c,color:#fff

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Since every value is between one and n, I can treat each value as a pointer to another index. This forms an implicit linked list. The duplicate value means two different indices point to the same location, which creates a cycle. The entry point of that cycle is the duplicate number.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: I use Floyd's tortoise and hare algorithm. The slow pointer moves one step: slow equals nums at slow. The fast pointer moves two steps: fast equals nums at nums at fast. They will meet inside the cycle.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: After they meet, I reset one pointer to index zero and move both one step at a time. The point where they meet again is the cycle entrance, which is the duplicate value. In our example, the cycle entrance is index three, so the answer is three.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Excellent. This gives O of n time and O of one space, and it doesn't modify the array. That's the optimal solution.

sections.title: Summary
sections.diagram:
graph LR
    subgraph Comparison["Approach Comparison"]
        A["HashSet\nO(n) / O(n)"] --> B["Binary Search\nO(n log n) / O(1)"]
        B --> C["Floyd's Cycle\nO(n) / O(1)"]
    end
    style A fill:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style B fill:#a78bfa,color:#fff
    style C fill:#fb923c,color:#fff

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Great work. You showed three approaches: HashSet with linear time and space, binary search on the value range trading time for constant space, and Floyd's cycle detection achieving both linear time and constant space.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: The key insight was recognizing that the array values can be treated as pointers, forming an implicit linked list. The duplicate creates a cycle, and finding the cycle entry gives us the answer. This technique is worth remembering for any problem involving values that map to valid indices.
